Member-only story

Hard links and symbolic links both let you reach a file in more than one way. That’s where their similarities end. Understanding the difference will save you from one of the most common mistakes Linux beginners make.

3 min read
Just now

--

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Photo by D koi on UnsplashIn the previous two episodes, we discovered that Linux separates a file’s identity from its filename. We learned that hard links allow multiple filenames to point to the same inode, and that deleting one of those names doesn’t necessarily delete the file.
Now it’s time to meet another kind of link.
One that behaves very differently, one that most Linux users encounter almost immediately.
The symbolic link.
At first glance, it looks like another way of creating multiple names for the same file. In reality, it’s built on a completely different idea.
Here’s What You’ll Learn
By the end of this article, you’ll understand:

• What a symbolic link really is.

• Why symbolic links are not hard links.
